Makes bass sound louder and chunkier without using extra volume headroom. It listens to your sub-bass and generates matching overtones your ears interpret as more bass. Great with small speakers and for staying loud without clipping.
Sounds below this frequency get enhanced

This is a multiband compressor/expander: it splits the sound into frequency bands and evens out volume differences: quiet parts come up, loud peaks get tamed. Push the graph up to make a frequency range consistently louder and fuller.
* Reaction speed: how fast it responds to volume changes. Faster = punchier but can distort deep bass. * Detail level: how finely it analyzes frequencies. Higher = more precise, uses more battery. * Analysis engine: the math used to split frequencies. The default is fine. Wavelets treat bass in a more natural, ear-like way. * Graph: drag bands up (+) to boost leveling loudness in that range, down (-) to reduce.

Restores sparkle and \"air\" to dull or compressed music. It listens to the upper mids and synthesizes new matching treble overtones above the chosen frequency, like ViPER4Android\'s Spectrum Extension.
New treble gets generated above this point
How much synthesized treble is mixed in. Subtle is best
Boosts low frequencies with a smart filter that adapts to how much bass the music already has, keeping it clean instead of muddy.
Simulates the warm, slightly saturated sound of vintage tube amplifiers. Adds gentle harmonic color.
Makes the stereo image feel wider (or narrower) by adjusting the difference between the left and right channels.
Blends a little of each ear\'s audio into the other, like listening to speakers in a room. Reduces headphone fatigue and makes old hard-panned mixes comfier.
Adds simulated room echo/space to the sound, from small room to concert hall.

Final volume stage. Post gain makes everything louder/quieter; the limiter decides what happens when audio would get too loud and distort. Soft saturation mode lets you push much louder while staying smooth.
Loads ViPER DDC (.vdc) correction files that reshape the sound for specific headphone models.

Applies an impulse response (IRS/WAV) file: a sound "fingerprint" that can simulate speakers, rooms, or custom EQ curves with studio-grade accuracy.

Advanced waveform editing takes six whole numbers split by semicolons, with no spaces:
1. Start level, in dB below the IR's loudest point. Shrink cuts off the quiet lead-in before the IR first gets louder than this.
2. End level, in dB below the loudest point. Both shrink modes cut off the tail after the IR last gets louder than this.
3 to 6. Delay for IR channels 1 to 4, in samples at the current processing rate. Each channel starts that many samples later. This works in every mode.
Example: -60;-90;0;20;0;0 trims more than the default (-80;-100;0;0;0;0) and delays channel 2 by 20 samples. Keep each delay well under the IR's length after any shrinking. A delay below 0, or one that is too long for the IR, makes the app ignore all six and use the default instead.

Makes music sound crisper and more detailed. Natural sharpens transients (attacks of notes), XHiFi lifts the treble shelf, and OZone+ does both.
Widens the stereo field like ViPER\'s Field Surround: surround strength pushes side content outward, mid image controls how forward the center (vocals) sits.
Keeps volume consistent automatically: quiet songs get gently boosted toward your target level, loud ones are left alone. Slow and smooth, no pumping.

Pulls the sound out of the middle of your head and places it in front of you: head-shadowed crossfeed with realistic ear-to-ear timing, multi-tap early reflections with a short room tail, and stereo widening. Headphones only. Try 60-90% strength. Inspired by ViPER\'s VHS+.

A fast, punchy studio-style compressor (like classic FET hardware): it tames peaks above the threshold so you can raise overall loudness. Lower threshold + higher ratio = more squeeze.
Gently blends softened sound between ears to reduce headphone listening fatigue on long sessions. Pick how strong the cure is.
The classic ViPER bass boost. Natural = clean shelf boost, Pure Bass+ = boost with warm harmonics, Subwoofer = focused punch at one frequency.
Symmetric filters with constant group delay. Off uses minimum phase, which adds no latency and is usually the better choice for listening.

Classic is the original ViPER room. Plate is a smooth, dense studio plate. Concert hall is a large, warm space with a long tail. Room adds early reflections for a natural, believable space. The smooth versions of Concert hall and Room are rebuilt to lose the metallic ring: a denser tail with no repeating echoes.
ViPER-style room reverb: adds space and echo. Room size sets how big the space feels, damping softens the tail, width spreads it in stereo, wet/dry balance effect vs original.
Tunes sound for tiny phone speakers: removes lows they can\'t play anyway (saving power and rattle) and lifts presence so voices cut through.

A full echo unit: repeats with feedback, a filter inside the feedback loop so each repeat gets darker, tape-style modulation, diffusion to smear the tail, and saturation. Ping-pong bounces repeats between your ears, which is lovely on headphones.

Shifts the pitch of everything up or down without changing playback speed: deep-voice, chipmunk, or subtle retunes in half-semitone steps. A slight watery shimmer at extreme settings is normal for real-time shifting.

Granular is instant and costs nothing, but wobbles a little on held notes. Smooth listens to each frequency separately and keeps them steady, which sounds far cleaner on sustained music, at the cost of about 20ms of delay and a bit more work for the phone. Signalsmith is built in and handles gliding notes and full mixes more smoothly still, but everything comes out about 0.15 seconds late, so on videos the sound trails the picture, and very low notes can land a little off pitch. The two Rubber Band methods need the free add-on below. The methods that keep voice character stop voices going chipmunky or giant.

When enhanced processing is enabled, you can selectively exclude certain apps from being processed by RootlessViPER4Android. Use the 3-dot menu on the bottom right corner and select 'Excluded apps' to access this feature.

While legacy mode is disabled, RootlessViPER4Android relies on media apps to send a system broadcast when they start playback. This is an advantage over legacy mode because each app gets its own effect engine assigned to it, which allows for more fine-grained control. Otherwise, with legacy mode turned on, all apps would share a single processing engine, which Android deprecates and should not be used anymore.

Unfortunately, not all media apps do this correctly and, therefore, would not function correctly with legacy mode disabled. To solve this issue, you can enable enhanced processing. Instead of relying on system broadcasts about new media sessions, RootlessViPER4Android will proactively scan for media sessions by itself and allow proper support for uncooperative media apps.

Picks a frequency range and distorts only that, leaving the rest of the music alone. The graph is the filter that chooses the range. The card opens with one low-pass corner, so by default it distorts the bass and nothing else. Peaking and shelf handles shape what goes in instead of selecting a range outright, so the full equaliser is still available here. Eight distortion characters, a chorus on the distorted band, and a mix control over the whole thing.
Band graph, distortion character and chorus

Which curve Character uses to round peaks. Smooth starts bending straight away, so it adds the most density and warmth. Hard stays linear until the very top, so it leaves quiet detail alone and only clips the peaks. Classic sits between them. Does nothing while Character is at zero.

The ways a tape machine fails, offered as colour. Wow is slow speed drift from a tired capstan; flutter is the same fault ten times quicker, heard as shimmer on held notes. Saturation is tape running out of headroom gently instead of clipping. Bias set low makes a machine brighter and grittier, set high it goes dull. The head bump is the low resonance that makes tape masters sound weightier than the mix did.
Slow pitch drift, well under a cycle a second.
The quick version, heard as shimmer on sustained notes.
How hard the tape is driven. Rounds peaks and adds harmonics rather than clipping.
Below zero is under-biased: brighter and grittier. Above zero is over-biased: duller. Flat in the middle.
The low resonance around 60 Hz a tape head produces.
How much of the tape signal is blended back in. At 0%% nothing is changed at all.

Which ear the sound sits in. Useful for uneven hearing, a headphone with a tired driver, or one earbud that is simply quieter than the other. Balance cuts the far side rather than boosting the near one, so it never costs headroom or pushes the limiter. Mono blends the two channels together, which is what you want if you are listening with a single earbud. Otherwise anything panned to the other side is lost.
Left at the bottom, right at the top, centred in the middle.
For a miswired cable, an adapter, or a recording that came out the wrong way round.
Mixes the channels together. At 100%% both ears hear everything, which is the one to use with a single earbud.

Keeps the volume even from one song to the next. It listens to the last few seconds the way streaming services measure loudness (LUFS, ITU-R BS.1770) and slowly turns the volume up or down towards the target. It never turns up during a pause or near silence. When there is a gap of about half a second or more between songs, a boost is let go and a cut is kept, so the next song is judged on its own and a loud one never starts boosted. Songs that run straight into each other (gapless albums, crossfade) leave no gap to notice, so there the volume follows more slowly. The slower the speed, the more of the loud and quiet parts within a song it leaves alone.
-14 LUFS is where most streaming services put music. Lower is quieter.
How far a quiet song may be turned up.
How far a loud song may be turned down.
Slow: listens to 20 seconds, the gentlest
Fast: listens to 4 seconds, also evens out parts of a song
Never boosts so far that the loudest recent peak would reach the output limiter, so loud moments are not squashed by the limiter.

Fine volume steps. Android gives media about fifteen volume steps, several dB apart, which is too coarse for quiet listening. While this is on and audio is being processed, the system media volume stays where it is and the volume keys move a fine control instead, half a dB per press, about two hundred steps from full down to silence. Holding a key speeds it up. When a step needs more than the system volume allows, the system volume goes up one step and the fine control makes up the rest. Switching this off, or stopping processing, puts the system volume back where it was. When processing starts again the fine level picks up where it was, unless the system volume or the output changed in the meantime; switching off starts it over. Apps that are not processed keep playing at the system volume. During calls, while ringing and when nothing is playing, the keys work as usual.

Allow ViPER4Android to appear on top, then come back
Lets the volume keys move ViPER4Android\'s smooth volume in half dB steps. Only takes the keys while smooth volume is on, audio is being processed and media is playing. Reads no screen content.

The noises a record makes, as separate controls. Vintage tape models a machine that is working badly: drifting in pitch, running out of headroom. This models a worn disc, which fails differently: it adds things that were never in the recording. Everything here except Wear is a noise mixed alongside the music, so with every control at zero nothing is added at all.
The continuous bed a record sits on. Band-limited, because a groove reproduces neither the very top nor the very bottom.
How often the small dull ticks of worn vinyl happen.
How big each one is. A lot of small crackle is a tired record; a little large crackle is a damaged one.
Rare and much louder, from a scratch or a speck of grit. Rings rather than just ticking.
Very short and bright: a dust particle rather than a scratch. Reads as an edge instead of an event.
Dense high-frequency frying: a record played wet, or worn smooth. Crackle fast enough to stop being separate events.
Flat, quiet and always there. The noise floor of the cutting chain rather than the disc.
Sharp, thin, upper-mid ticks: the prickly quality of a dirty stylus.
The motor and bearing underneath everything. Felt more than heard.
The only control that touches the music itself: high end lost to a worn groove.
A real record crackles constantly, which is what you want while music plays, but obviously synthetic in a silence. Turn this up and the noise fades with the music.
How much of the record is blended back in. At 0%% nothing is changed at all.

Adds harmonics that were never in the recording, which the ear reads as detail and weight. Four ranges, each with its own amount, so you can put air on top without also making the bass fuzzy. Character picks the flavour: Warm, Retro and Tape are symmetrical and add odd harmonics (the transistor end); Tube and Triode are lopsided and add even ones, which is the valve sound. The existing Bass exciter card is the older two-band bass-only version and still works; this replaces it for new setups.
Warm, Retro and Tape add odd harmonics; Tube and Triode are asymmetric and add even ones, which sounds fuller and less edgy.
How hard each range is pushed into the shaper. More drive means richer harmonics for the same amount added.
How much of the excited signal is blended back in. At 0%% nothing is changed at all.

Three things for the bottom of the spectrum. The subsonic filter throws away rumble below anything you can hear, which is pure wasted headroom pushing the limiter around. Weight is one knob for body. Mud eases back the region where recordings pile up and turn thick. Folding bass to mono lives in the stereo imaging card, and putting punch back into a kick lives in Impact. Neither is repeated here.
Removes everything below this, steeply. Set to 0 to switch it off.
Body added or taken away below the frequency underneath.
A wide dip where recordings turn thick. Negative thins it out.
How much of the treated signal is blended back in. At 0%% nothing is changed at all.

Adds new notes an octave and more below the bass, the way a subwoofer that is not there would. It follows the bass line note by note and plays a clean tone locked to it at half its pitch, a third, a quarter and so on, rising and dying away with it. It listens to the bass in the middle of the mix, which is where bass sits, and adds the same to both ears. Anything that would land below about 20 Hz is left out, since all it would do there is cost headroom. Best on headphones or speakers that reach low: on a phone speaker it mostly takes loudness away.
An octave and a fifth down (f/3)
Two octaves and a third down (f/5)
Two octaves and a fifth down (f/6)
Two octaves and a seventh down (f/7)
Three octaves and a second down (f/9)
Three octaves and a third down (f/10)
Only the bass under this is followed. Lower sticks to the deepest notes; higher also follows bass lines that sit further up.
How much of the new notes is added. At 0%% nothing is added, and with the output level at 0 dB the sound goes through untouched.
The level of everything once the new notes are in. Turn it down to make room for them, so the limiter does not have to.

Shapes how a note starts and how long it takes to die, rather than how loud it is. Two envelope followers chase the signal at different speeds, and the gap between them says which part of a note you are in, so a held tone comes through completely untouched while a drum hit can be sharpened or softened. Use it to put the snap back into over-compressed music, or to take the room off a boomy recording.
Above zero sharpens the start of each note, below zero softens it.
Above zero lets notes ring on, below zero shortens their tails.
Everything below this is shaped by the Low controls.
Everything above this is shaped by the High controls.
The most any range may ever be moved. Zero switches the whole effect off.
How much of the shaped signal is blended back in. At 0%% nothing is changed at all.

Width, but chosen per frequency range instead of all at once. The plain widener pulls the bass apart along with everything else, which thins the centre and falls apart in mono; here the low end can be folded to mono while the top opens up. Mono recordings are left exactly as they are, whatever the settings.
Everything under this is folded to the centre. Set to 0 to leave the bass alone.
1.0 leaves the range untouched, below narrows toward the centre, above widens.
How much of the reshaped image is blended back in. At 0%% nothing is changed at all.

Bands that only act when the music asks. A static cut is always there, so taming a boom that happens on four notes costs body on everything else; each band here watches its own slice of the spectrum and moves only while that slice is over its threshold. Ships tuned to tame low boom, harshness and sibilance.
Where this band listens, and where it acts.
The level this band has to reach before it does anything.
The most it may ever change. Negative cuts, positive lifts; zero switches the band off.
How narrow the band is. Wider sounds gentler, narrower is more surgical.

As the volume goes down, your ears lose the bass first and some of the treble with it, so quiet music sounds thin. This puts them back by as much as the volume went down, following the phone\'s media volume as you change it. At the reference volume it does nothing at all. It never boosts, so it brings the bass and treble forward by turning the rest down, and that is a lot quieter: 30 dB under the reference, the middle loses about 35 dB more with the Classic method and about 16 dB with ISO. Set the reference first, by playing something at the volume you usually listen at and tapping the button below, then turn the phone up to make up the level.
Reads the volume every time it changes, and the level of Smooth volume while that is on. Turn off to set the listening volume yourself below.
The volume to correct for while the media volume is not followed.
Use the current volume as the reference
Play something you know at the volume where it sounds right, then tap this.
The media volume where the music already sounds full. 0 dB is the phone at full volume.
Moves the reference for headphones that are louder or quieter than usual at the same volume.
How much of the correction is applied. 100 percent is the full amount.
How quickly the bass rises as the volume falls. At 55 percent it rises 1.2 dB for every dB of volume.
How quickly the treble rises as the volume falls.
How loud the reference volume sounds, in phon. 80 is loud listening; lower it if your reference is quieter.
Cut what is too low to hear
Takes out rumble below the frequency set here, so the bass lift does not spend headroom on it.
6 dB per octave for each step.
0.707 is the smoothest. Higher values add a bump just above the frequency.

Headphones only. Places the music around you instead of inside your head: the main sound in front, and the room sound of the recording spread to the sides, behind you and a little above. It works out what is room sound from how alike the two channels are, so any ordinary stereo recording works. Speakers can\'t do this, so it switches itself off on the phone\'s speaker. Turn off Crossfeed and Headphone surround while this is on, and if your phone has its own Spatial audio switched on, turn one of the two off, or the effect is doubled. Adds about 22 ms of delay, which is fine for music and for video.
How much of the sound is placed around you. At 0 you hear the normal stereo, only delayed.
Moves sound that is panned hard to one side further out, from 30 toward 60 degrees.
How much of the recording\'s room sound goes to the sides and behind you.
How much of it goes above you. Height is the hardest direction to fake, so expect a gentle effect.
Adds a small room around you, which helps the sound feel outside your head. At 0 there is none.

Takes out the colour every direction of a measured set shares, such as the measuring speaker and the dummy head\'s ear canal. Leave it on unless a set says it is already evened out.

Free SOFA sets are listed at sofacoustics.org; a set measured on your own ears sounds best of all. Each set has its own licence, so check it before sharing. Sets measured in a room are cut to their first few milliseconds; use the Room slider instead.
Switches itself off while the sound comes from the phone\'s speaker or HDMI. Bluetooth and USB count as headphones.

Finds the voice in whatever is playing with a small speech model (GTCRN) that runs on the phone, then lets you turn everything else down for clearer dialogue in films, shows and podcasts, or turn the voice itself down for a karaoke track. The model only hears up to 8 kHz, so anything above that, the voice\'s own hiss and sparkle included, counts as background. It works before every other effect and adds about 34 ms of delay. Video apps do not know about that delay, so speech can trail the picture very slightly. Uses some battery while it is on.
How far everything that is not voice is turned down. At 100%% only the voice is left.
Turns the voice itself down, for a karaoke version. Set Reduce background to 0%% for that.
Raises the voice on top of the mix.
Lets the background back up between lines, so music and effects are not held down while nobody is talking.

Finds frequencies that suddenly stick out, like a harsh cymbal, a sharp \"s\" or a bright peak in some earphones, and turns them down only while they stick out. Everything else passes through untouched. Clean, steady notes are left alone on purpose, which also means a ring that only happens along with a held note is left alone too. Switch on Catch steady tones too if that is what bothers you. This card delays the sound by about 21 ms at 48 kHz and 23 ms at 44.1 kHz, which is fine for music and for video.
The most any frequency can be turned down. At 0 nothing is changed.
How far a frequency has to stand above its neighbours before it is turned down. Higher catches smaller bumps. At 60 percent it is 4 dB.
How quickly it reacts and lets go. Faster catches short bursts, slower sounds smoother.
What counts as sticking out: a narrow spike, or a wider stretch of harshness.
Only frequencies between these two are touched. Harshness mostly lives between 2 and 10 kHz.
Centre only works on vocals and lead instruments, edges only on what is spread wide.
Also turns down held notes that stick out, like a whistly synth or a ringing note. Off by default, so clean notes stay exactly as they are.
Plays only the part being taken away, so you can hear what the card is doing. Switch it off again for normal listening.
Centre-only catches a vocal without dulling the reverb around it; edges-only tames a wide, harsh mix without touching the lead.
How much of the corrected signal is blended back in. At 0%% nothing is changed at all.

Drag a handle to move it, long-press empty space to add one, long-press a handle to remove it. Low pass and high pass handles select a range; peaking and shelf handles shape what goes into the distortion.

Makes the music louder without letting it go past a ceiling you choose. The output limiter is a safety net that stops the signal leaving the rails; this is the tool for deliberately pushing into one. Gain drives the signal in, the ceiling is the hard stop, and character decides how much of the reduction is done by rounding peaks off rather than turning everything down around them. True peak measures the level between samples, which is where clipping hides from ordinary meters.
How hard the signal is driven into the ceiling. This is the loudness control.
Nothing leaves above this, whatever else is set. Leave a little headroom for lossy playback.
How quickly the level returns after a peak. Short is punchy and pumps; long is smooth and duller.
Trades clean gain reduction for saturation. Louder and warmer, at the cost of added harmonics.
Lets the leading edge of a hit through before the reduction lands, so drums keep their attack.

Measures the level between samples, not just at them, so peaks that only appear once a converter reconstructs the waveform are caught too. Needs oversampling, and switches it on by itself if it is off.
How much a peak on one side turns the other down with it. Full keeps the stereo image still; none reduces less but lets it wander.

Makes your headphones sound like a target curve. Pick your headphones (or load a measurement), pick the sound you want, and this works out the graphic EQ curve that gets you there. The result replaces the graphic EQ\'s current curve, and you can still edit it there afterwards.\n\nMeasurements and targets are downloaded from the AutoEq project only when you pick one. You can also load your own files: CSV or text with a frequency and a level on each line, REW exports and AutoEq files all work.

Use a measurement of your own
No raw measurement is published for this one, so it is estimated from its AutoEQ profile. Expect it to be close, not exact.
Use a target curve of your own
Each target was made for one kind of measuring rig. Using it with a different one can make the result a bit off.
Below this the correction fades out. Handy when the bass of a measurement depends on how well the headphones seal.
Above this the correction fades out. Treble measurements of in-ear headphones change with every fit, so about 10 kHz leaves that part alone.
Fills deep, narrow dips only part of the way. They usually move every time you put the headphones on, and filling them fully wastes volume and can ring.
